newsitem.title: USA: US thrifts diversifying but retain mortgage focus.
newsitem.headline: US thrifts diversifying but retain mortgage focus.

text.p: U.S. savings and loan institutions plan to diversify into commercial and consumer lending over the next five years, but will retain a primary focus on the mortgage sector, according to a survey released Tuesday by an industry trade group.
Real estate loans will likely decline from 91 percent of all thrift loans to about 82 percent in five years, said Paul Taylor, senior economist for America's Community Bankers.
"We're not getting out of that business," Taylor said at a press briefing. "We're simply growing in some other areas and we're still largely real estate related in our activities."

Congress is considering eliminating the federal thrift charter and forcing savings and loans to operate like banks. A bill approved by the House Banking Committee would phase out thrifts over several years.

The thrift industry strongly opposes the phase-out, but banks are demanding the provision be included. The bill is a long way from becoming law, however, and the proposal could be changed as it wends it way through the legislative process.
Taylor said the survey reaffirmed the special role of thrifts in the real estate market. Thrifts "are still serving the classic purposes that they were chartered for," he said.

Thrift loan portfolios will be comprised of about 12 percent of consumer loans, such as home equity and credit card loans, in five years, up from seven percent currently, Taylor said. Commercial and industrial loans will rise to six percent of all loans from two percent today.
The survey found that almost 11 percent of thrifts plan to begin offering home equity lines of credit, in addition to the 70 percent already active in the sector.
Other areas expected to attract at least five percent of thrifts were indirect consumer lending through dealers and personal unsecured loans.
Only 22 percent of thrifts securitize and sell mortgage loans currently, but another nine percent plan to do so in the future, the survey found.
And almost nine percent of thrifts plan to begin offering reverse mortgages, up from just six percent now.
Thrifts are also planning a big push into electronic and Internet banking, the survey found.

Just five percent offer home banking on a personal computer, but 30 percent plan to offer the service soon. And only three percent offer Internet banking, but 29 percent forsee offering cyberbanking evetually.
